terms.gloss: tire out, exhaust; passive, be worn out
evidence: Caes. B.G. 7.41.2: nostrōsque assiduō labōre dēfatīgārent (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: frequent and classical, where the simple fatīgāre is rare before Augustus. The participle dēfatīgātus is “exhausted” (see tired for the everyday fessus); dēfatīgārī with a negative is “never to tire of” (Cic. de Or. 3.145).

evidence: Liv. 1.23.9: ut fessōs cōnfectōsque aggrediantur (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Rab. Perd. 21: cōnfectus senectūte (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Its first sense is “finish, make, complete”; in the participle cōnfectus, with or without an ablative of the cause (age, illness, wounds, worry), it is “worn out, exhausted”.

evidence: Sall. Cat. 27.2: neque īnsomniīs neque labōre fatīgārī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Not frequent before Augustus (Lewis & Short); in prose dēfatīgāre is commoner.

phrases.english: I’ve been foiled, but I’m not worn out.

phrases.latin: opus faciam, ut dēfatīger ūsque, ingrātiīs ut dormiam
phrases.english: I’ll work till I’m quite worn out, so that I sleep whether I like it or not

sources: Lewis & Short: defatigo · Lewis & Short: conficio · Lewis & Short: fatigo
Terence (And. 669) from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-terentius); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.
